# Operator Chaining
<!-- Slide 50 -->

## Chains You Already Wrote? {.smaller}

- `Sales total = a + b + c;` (07.01)
- `cout << a << b;` (07.02)
- `return *this;` in `operator=` (08.02)

::: notes
Slides 51–60


:::

<!-- Slide 51 -->

---

## Two Kinds of Chains

| Operator | Changes its left operand? | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `+` | No | A new object, by value |
| `=` and `+=` | Yes | The left operand, by reference |
| `<<` | Yes, the stream | The stream, by reference |

- Each link in a chain works on whatever the previous link returned.

::: notes

:::

<!-- Slide 52 -->

---

## Why `<<` Must Return a Reference

- `cout << a << b` groups as `(cout << a) << b`.
- The second `<<` must write to the same stream as the first.
- Streams cannot be copied, so returning `ostream` by value does not compile.

::: notes
g++ rejects an operator<< that takes and returns ostream by value: the stream's copy constructor is not accessible. The reference is not a style choice here; it is the only option.
:::

<!-- Slide 53 -->

---

## You Have Written `return *this` Before

~~~cpp
Temperature& operator+=(const Temperature& rhs) {
    celsius += rhs.celsius;
    return *this;
}
~~~

| Part | Why |
|---|---|
| `Temperature&` | Hands back the object itself, not a copy |
| `const Temperature& rhs` | The right side is read, never changed |
| `return *this;` | `this` points to the left operand; `*this` is that object |

::: notes
Students wrote the same three parts in 08.02's copy assignment operator. Frame this as why that code works rather than as new syntax.
:::

<!-- Slide 54 -->

---

## `+=` That Chains

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}
~~~cpp
class Temperature {
private:
    double celsius;

public:
    Temperature(double value = 0.0) { celsius = value; }

    Temperature& operator+=(const Temperature& rhs) {
        celsius += rhs.celsius;
        return *this;
    }

    friend ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const Temperature& t);
};

int main() {
    Temperature a(20.0);
    Temperature b(5.0);

    cout << (a += b) << " " << a << endl;
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

Output: `25 25`

::: notes
Both values are 25 because (a += b) is a itself. The definition of operator<< is in the full program.

Never return a reference to a local variable: an operator+ that returns Temperature& to its local result leaves a dangling reference, and g++ warns with -Wreturn-local-addr.

Full program: cpp/plus_equal_chain.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 55 -->

---

## Chaining Setters

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}
~~~cpp
class Roster {
private:
    string name;
    int seats;

public:
    explicit Roster(int capacity) { name = "Unnamed"; seats = capacity; }

    Roster& setName(const string& value) { name = value; return *this; }
    Roster& setCapacity(int value) { seats = value; return *this; }

    void print() const { cout << name << ": " << seats << " seats" << endl; }
};

int main() {
    Roster section(25);
    section.setName("CISP 400").setCapacity(30);
    section.print();
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::: notes
Output: CISP 400: 30 seats

The same return *this lets member functions chain. Reading: learncpp 15.1, The hidden this pointer and member function chaining.

Full program: cpp/roster_setters.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 56 -->

---

## Where Did Capacity 30 Go?

~~~cpp
Roster setName(const string& value) { name = value; return *this; }
Roster setCapacity(int value) { seats = value; return *this; }

Roster section(25);
section.setName("CISP 400").setCapacity(30);
section.print();
~~~

. . .

Output: `CISP 400: 25 seats`

::: notes
The only change from the previous slide is the missing & on both return types. Ask students to predict the output.
:::

<!-- Slide 57 -->

---

## The Copy Took the Change

| Call | Runs on | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `setName("CISP 400")` | `section` | A copy of `section` |
| `.setCapacity(30)` | The copy | Another copy, then discarded |

- `section` got its name but never its capacity.
- The fix is one character on each return type: `Roster&`.

::: notes
This bug compiles, runs, and prints a wrong answer, which is exactly the kind of bug the unit tests in the next topic catch.
:::

<!-- Slide 58 -->

---

## Value or Reference?

| The operator or member function | Returns |
|---|---|
| Changes the object it was called on: `=`, `+=`, `<<`, setters | `*this` by reference |
| Produces a new value: `+`, `-`, `*` | A new object by value |

- Never return a reference to a local variable.

::: notes

:::

<!-- Slide 59 -->

---

## Summary

- Return `*this` by reference when a call changes its object, so the next link works on the same object.
- Return by value when a call builds a new value; a by-value return in a chain silently works on a copy.

::: notes

:::
